messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

The flood came at night. Marcus was eighteen, working the closing shift at a burger chain near the river, when the sirens started. He and two coworkers tried to sandbag the back door, but the water rose too fast—brown, cold, and smelling of diesel and rot. They climbed onto the walk-in freezer, and for four hours Marcus sat in the dark, listening to the current slam debris against the walls, certain the building would collapse. When rescue boats finally came, he had to wade through chest-deep water, the chemical stench so thick he could taste it. He made it out, but something in him did not.

In the months that followed, Marcus found he could not stop seeing it. The memories came as pictures—the black water, the freezer door buckling—and when they did, the same raw terror flooded his chest, as if he were still perched on that metal box. Sometimes, without warning, he would catch a whiff of diesel or wet concrete, and the whole scene would snap back into his senses, vivid and suffocating. He had come to believe that he was permanently damaged by that night, that the person he used to be—easygoing, quick to laugh—had been erased. "I used to be happy," he told his therapist during the first session. "Now I'm just miserable all the time. I don't even recognize myself."

This belief that he was broken shaped everything Marcus did. He began to rehearse conversations in his head before any interaction, running through what he might say and what the other person might respond, because he was certain that his real self would say the wrong thing and reveal how hollow he had become. At work, the fryer oil smelled too much like gasoline, and the hiss of the pressure washer reminded him of the flood, so he started calling in sick on busy nights, avoiding anything that could feel stressful. He tried hard not to think about the trauma, pushing the images away whenever they surfaced, but the effort itself made him feel exhausted and defective—proof that he was not getting better, that the damage was permanent. Each time he suppressed a memory and failed, the belief that he was unrecognizably changed grew stronger, and the next time a smell or a sound triggered a flash of terror, he was even more convinced that he would never be the person he used to be.

His avoidance cost him shifts, then his schedule, then his social life. He stopped answering texts from friends because he did not know what to say. The rehearsed conversations never felt real. One evening, a coworker mentioned the anniversary of the flood, and Marcus felt his throat close; he walked out mid-shift and did not go back for three days. He told himself it was better to isolate than to let anyone see how far he had fallen. The person he had become was a stranger even to himself—miserable, watchful, always bracing for the next memory to hit. He had lost his job at the burger chain, and his mother finally made him an appointment. What frightened Marcus most was not the memories themselves anymore, but the growing suspicion that the person he was now was all he would ever be. He came to the clinic hoping, against everything he believed, that maybe he was wrong.
